title: A Voice From Nowhere • zanlib
excerpt: The remnants of human understanding in generated content.
content_html:
24 July 2026

The Holy See has had a website since 1995, but the day Pope Leo XIV’s first encyclical went up was the first time I saw it being linked to from outside the niche Catholic circles. The link to the encyclical made rounds on X, LinkedIn, Hacker News, and Reddit, and it was the first ever “.va” link published to lobste.rs. I was surprised to see it was upvoted. People seemed to have actually read it. And they seemed to argue about it in good faith.

I suspect that if you had told a room of engineers fifteen years ago, a time when Dawkins was still a frequent sight on airport shelves, that one day they’d be reading a Catholic encyclical and mostly nodding along, you’d have been at best met with polite disbelief.

Papal encyclicals, over the centuries, became documents that garner interest not just internally, from Catholic theologians and clergy. They became serious works of moral philosophy read and discussed outside the Catholic or even Christian circles. As such, besides being a source of magisterial teaching for Catholics, they have to stand on their own merits as addressed to “all people of good will.”1Marginnote mh21Pope Leo XIV. Magnifica humanitas. Libreria Editrice Vaticana 2026; § 2 ↩ The first time I saw this with my own eyes was with the publication of Pope Francis’s Laudato Si’. While the subject of that one was not of particular interest to me, it sparked widespread action and over time diffused into many initiatives. Outside of the many strictly Catholic institutions it permeated, it was quoted during UN panels on ecology and cited in serious climate change papers2Marginnote ls2McCallum, M. L. Perspective: Global country-by-country response of public interest in the environment to the papal encyclical, Laudato Si’. Biological Conservation 2019; pp. 209–225 ↩ published in multidisciplinary journals.

The election of Pope Leo was a deeply personal event for me. I was born during the pontificate of John Paul II, whose legacy still endures in Polish culture to this day. At the time of the election of Benedict XVI, I was still a child; at the time of his retirement I was a disinterested teenager. Francis died on Easter Monday, and I learned about it that day while listening to the radio on my way to church. Two weeks later the entire family looked at the live feed from the EWTN covering the conclave, chuckling at the seagulls. And then we had a new Pope.

Leo is the first pontiff that I will most likely follow consciously for the entirety of his rule, and at the time of his election I promised myself I will make a wholehearted attempt at reading what he writes. The fact that Magnifica humanitas concerns a subject that I work with day-to-day, and am actually interested in, is just an excellent concurrence.

I thought about writing a complete commentary on the encyclical, but about midway through I figured that it might not actually be that good an idea—the document is so expansive and touches on so many subjects that it’s impossible to comment on everything coherently while keeping to the perspective proper to my own trade. There are, however, individual threads running through it that are very relevant to the field of programming and the everyday work of software engineers, which are worth exploring. While my work is not in the field of AI, I use these tools every day extensively, and there is one property of them that the Pope identified, which most of our field seems content to ignore.

A voice that belongs to no one

The encyclical hands us one of its many theses early:

“In practice, however, technology is never neutral, because it takes on the characteristics of those who devise, finance, regulate and use it.”3Marginnote mh93Magnifica humanitas, § 9 ↩

That a tool takes on the character of its makers is nothing new, but the people who build these machines have a very particular one. They are the heirs and priests of Western rationalism, of the subject-object split, of classical dualism, which is so ingrained that it no longer registers as a position at all. It is the conviction that if a man works hard enough to divorce himself from his prejudices, his moods, his circumstances, his biases, what’s left when the subtraction is finished is the world seen plain, true, factual, and objective.

A mindset so ubiquitous that there is no getting away from it.

“[This] kind of rationality has been used since antiquity to remove oneself from the tedium and depression of one’s immediate surroundings. What makes it hard to see is that where once it was used to get away from it all, the escape has been so successful that now it is the ‘it all’ that the romantics are trying to escape.”4Marginnote zmm4Pirsig, R. Zen and the Art of Motorcycle Maintenance. Vintage 2004; pp. 65–66 ↩

“The apparent objectivity of the responses,” the Pope writes, “can lead us to overlook the fact that they reflect the cultural assumptions of those who designed and trained them.”5Marginnote mh1005Magnifica humanitas, § 100 ↩ The pretense of standing nowhere in particular is not the absence of a bias, but a bias of its own, one that the builders hold, hidden well enough that they have hidden it from themselves. There is only one point of view that has any claim to be objective, and is not accessible directly to any of us.

However, the confident voice of the language model is not the sound of having arrived there. It is hollower still, because when a human sets out on a road towards objectivity, we can see the attempt under the surface of what is written. In the case of machine-generated prose and code, there is no such striving underneath.

The path underneath

“These systems merely imitate certain functions of human intelligence. In doing so, they often surpass human intelligence in speed and computational capacity, offering tangible benefits across many fields. Yet this power remains entirely tied to data processing. (…) They may imitate language, behavior and analytical skills, or even simulate empathy and understanding, but they do not understand what they produce, for they lack the affective, relational and spiritual perspective through which human beings grow in wisdom.”6Marginnote mh996Magnifica humanitas, § 99 ↩

Pirsig spends a good part of Chapter 6 of Zen and the Art of Motorcycle Maintenance taking a motorcycle apart in a few different ways.7Marginnote zmm27Z&AMM, pp. 66–68 ↩ The divisions he draws are not welded into the machine. There is no single correct way to carve a motorcycle into parts; a person chooses where to cut, and he chooses according to what he already understands, what he has seen fail before, what he happens to care about. A rider might be concerned with the split according to the function, a mechanic might be concerned with the split according to its constituent assembly, a parts vendor might studiously follow the factory-prescribed parts numbering scheme to make a split of his own. The manual that ships with the machine hides all of this, written as it is in the impersonal spectator’s voice, as though no one stood behind it—though of course someone did. Motorcycles were not found lying in a field. People made them run, and the making left a trail.

That trail is what I mean when I say that human work has a path underneath it, there is a structure of thought that underpins everything we make. When you write by hand, something prompted you to write it a certain way; that path is inherent to you, your perspective on the problem, your prior experience, your particular circumstances. You sort the grains of sand8Marginnote zmm38Z&AMM, p. 72 ↩ a certain way.

The machine has no such path—or rather, and this is the whole of the trouble, it pretends to one it does not have. AI parrots that structure, but because it “reasons” in a completely different way, it is unable to produce it on its own. The form is reproduced without the comprehension that generated it. It is a great pretender—again, that is what it is meant to be, to a degree—and so when you read AI-generated content, be it prose or code, there is often a certain uneasiness. The content might be correct in every meaningful sense, it looks right, but at the same time it seems completely devoid of any underlying structure. Humans naturally think, reason, experience, and talk using analogy; above a certain minimal threshold of quality, it is clear that there is some kind of structure behind the writing, and that structure is what the machine cannot lay down.

The path is not wholly absent. When you generate code or prose, some knowledge has to be put into that generation, and that input—that is, the agent prompt, in most cases—is an artefact that has a path underneath it like any other piece of human creative work. What is hard is that when reviewing AI-generated code or reading AI-generated prose, you’re getting the output rather than the input, and the further the two are divorced—the wider the gap between the last point of human judgement and the finished artefact—the harder it becomes to make out what that path was, or if indeed there was one in the first place.

When you read, you’re looking, by reflex, for the structure underneath—why here and not there, what was seen and set aside, where the author was uncertain about his assumptions. When you cannot tell whether you are looking at the work of a careful writer, or a stochastic parrot, you cannot tell whether the structure is there to be found, or how much human intellect has been put into it. This is why reading anything you’ve already clocked as AI is so exhausting. You are guessing, and looking for something that you don’t know is even there to be found.

Foreclosed on the way in

If the tool erases the path in the work, it also, more slowly, erases the path in the worker.

“The speed and ease with which answers or summaries can be obtained risk extinguishing the desire to ask questions (…) As Plato wrote, the deepest and most important things are learned only after much time and effort (…) ‘striking upon’ ideas (…) like flint until the spark of understanding is kindled.”9Marginnote mh1409Magnifica humanitas, § 140 ↩

When you have a specific engineering issue that needs fixing, ordinarily you would consult the manual, or the documentation, or some other relevant literature, and try to find the solution there. While doing this, you would often stumble on additional, unrelated information that you would file away, half-consciously, ready to be used when the need arose. Searching with Google removed some of that serendipity, directing you to the one section that dealt with your problem—but you still landed on the page, and might still glance at something interesting on the way past.

A Google result is, at least, a whole document: it answers your question and also does three or four other things around the edges. An answer from a chatbot is trimmed to exactly the query, with no margins and no digressions. When your only interface to the codebase is the chat window, you don’t see what’s around the diffs. You foreclose on the lateral exploration by getting precisely what you asked for and nothing adjacent to it.

And when you no longer know what your code is doing and where the boundaries of your system are, you lose the ability to maintain the system. If the entire team maintaining the project disconnects from what actually gets deployed in production, that’s lights out.10Marginnote wsff10Horthy, D. Why Software Factories Fail ↩

The signature and what it hides

“This is where accountability becomes crucial: the possibility of identifying who must ‘account’ for decisions, justify them, monitor them, and, when necessary, challenge them and remedy any harm caused.”11Marginnote mh10511Magnifica humanitas, § 105 ↩

When I worked on a project for a large professional-services client, we had conventions to ensure that every line of code could be traced back to a person ultimately responsible for it: lines lived in commits labelled with Jira tickets, the tickets carried sign-offs from the subject matter expert who had made sure the requirements and the business logic were correct, and they lived inside larger epics signed-off on by a manager. When something failed badly enough, everyone in that chain got on a call and worked on a fix. Some of my colleagues thought this unhealthy, and said we ought to have blameless postmortems.

We have them these days: “oh, Claude wrote it like that. You have it too, just prompt it for a fix.”

There is, I have noticed, a great deal of effort now spent divorcing oneself from the machine’s output. Some of the people I work with do not want to acknowledge that a particular commit was written by AI, because to acknowledge it is to invite the question of whether they understood the problem at all. So they sign the commit with their own names, omit the Co-Authored-By, and leave it to the reader to decide whether he is looking at the work of a competent programmer or a language model. And it is impolite to suggest that a colleague’s work is AI-generated, since the suggestion implies he did not think. So the question is never asked. The whole thing dissolves, and we lose track of the level at which understanding last existed, before the work was handed off to the machine—or whether it was ever there in the first place.

This is precisely the possibility that the encyclical asks us to keep alive, “the possibility of identifying who must account for decisions.” The encyclical, discussing war, insists that “it is not permissible to entrust lethal or otherwise irreversible decisions to artificial systems.”12Marginnote mh19812Magnifica humanitas, § 198 ↩ The principle is not confined to the battlefield. All systems should have a chain of accountability that ultimately terminates in a person, even if just for reasons of respect and common courtesy, and the trouble with the voice from nowhere is that it lets the chain terminate in nothing while looking, for everyone else, as though it terminates in you.

The voice from nowhere is seductive for exactly the reason it is dangerous: it comes from nowhere, so there is no one to credit, no one to blame, and no one of whom to ask “how do you know that?” Technology, the Pope says, takes on the character of those who make it. What should trouble us is not the character it takes on, but how readily we have learned to build in a voice that admits to no maker at all.

blocks.html_en: Pirsig spends a good part of Chapter 6 of Zen and the Art of Motorcycle Maintenance taking a motorcycle apart in a few different ways.7Marginnote zmm27Z&AMM, pp. 66–68 ↩ The divisions he draws are not welded into the machine. There is no single correct way to carve a motorcycle into parts; a person chooses where to cut, and he chooses according to what he already understands, what he has seen fail before, what he happens to care about. A rider might be concerned with the split according to the function, a mechanic might be concerned with the split according to its constituent assembly, a parts vendor might studiously follow the factory-prescribed parts numbering scheme to make a split of his own. The manual that ships with the machine hides all of this, written as it is in the impersonal spectator’s voice, as though no one stood behind it—though of course someone did. Motorcycles were not found lying in a field. People made them run, and the making left a trail.

blocks.html_en: The machine has no such path—or rather, and this is the whole of the trouble, it pretends to one it does not have. AI parrots that structure, but because it “reasons” in a completely different way, it is unable to produce it on its own. The form is reproduced without the comprehension that generated it. It is a great pretender—again, that is what it is meant to be, to a degree—and so when you read AI-generated content, be it prose or code, there is often a certain uneasiness. The content might be correct in every meaningful sense, it looks right, but at the same time it seems completely devoid of any underlying structure. Humans naturally think, reason, experience, and talk using analogy; above a certain minimal threshold of quality, it is clear that there is some kind of structure behind the writing, and that structure is what the machine cannot lay down.

24 July 2026

罗马教廷自 1995 年起就有了一个网站，但在教皇利奥十四世的第一份通谕发布的那天，我第一次看到它与小众天主教圈子之外的人联系在一起。 该通谕的链接在 X、LinkedIn、Hacker News 和 Reddit 上流传，这是 lobste.rs 上发布的第一个“.va”链接。 我很惊讶地看到它被投票了。 人们似乎真的读过它。 他们似乎真诚地争论这个问题。

我怀疑，如果你在十五年前告诉一屋子的工程师，当时道金斯仍然经常出现在机场货架上，有一天他们会读一本天主教通谕，而且大多是点头附和，你充其量只会得到礼貌的怀疑。

几个世纪以来，教皇通谕不仅成为引起天主教神学家和神职人员内部兴趣的文件。 它们成为天主教甚至基督教圈子之外阅读和讨论的严肃的道德哲学著作。 因此，除了成为天主教徒权威教义的来源之外，他们还必须立足于自己的优点，向“所有善意的人”表达。1Marginnote mh21教皇利奥十四世。 伟大的人性。 梵蒂冈出版社 2026； § 2 ↩ 我第一次亲眼看到这一点是在教宗方济各的《愿祢受赞颂》出版时。 虽然我对这个主题并不是特别感兴趣，但它引发了广泛的行动，并随着时间的推移扩散到许多倡议中。 除了它渗透到许多严格的天主教机构之外，它还在联合国生态学小组中被引用，并在严肃的气候变化论文中被引用2Marginnote ls2McCallum，M. L。 观点：全球各国对环境公共利益对教皇通谕《愿祢受赞颂》的回应。 生物保护2019；页数 209–225 ↩ 发表在多学科期刊上。

教皇利奥的当选对我来说是一件非常个人化的事件。 我出生在约翰·保罗二世任教皇期间，他的遗产至今仍在波兰文化中延续。 当本笃十六世当选时，我还是个孩子；在他退休时，我还是一个无私的青少年。 弗朗西斯于复活节星期一去世，那天我在去教堂的路上听广播时得知了这一消息。 两周后，全家人看着 EWTN 报道秘密会议的直播，对着海鸥咯咯地笑。 然后我们有了一位新教皇。

利奥是第一位我很可能在整个统治期间有意识地追随的教皇，在他当选时，我向自己保证，我将全心全意地尝试阅读他所写的内容。 事实上，《Magnifica humanitas》涉及的是我日常工作的一个主题，而且我确实对此很感兴趣，这真是一个极好的契合。

我想过对通谕写一篇完整的评论，但在写到一半时，我发现这实际上可能不是一个好主意——该文件是如此广泛，涉及如此多的主题，以至于不可能在保持适合我自己行业的视角的同时对所有内容进行连贯的评论。 然而，其中运行的个别线程与编程领域和软件工程师的日常工作非常相关，值得探索。 虽然我的工作不是在人工智能领域，但我每天都广泛使用这些工具，教皇指出了它们的一个特性，而我们领域的大多数人似乎都愿意忽视这一特性。

不属于任何人的声音

通谕很早就向我们提出了众多论点之一：

“然而，在实践中，技术从来都不是中立的，因为它具有设计、融资、监管和使用技术的人的特征。”3Marginnote mh93Magnifica humanitas, § 9 ↩

一种工具具有其制造者的特征并不是什么新鲜事，但制造这些机器的人却有一个非常特殊的特征。 他们是西方理性主义、主客体分裂、古典二元论的继承者和传教士，这种二元论是如此根深蒂固，以至于根本不再被视为一种立场。 人们坚信，如果一个人足够努力，使自己摆脱偏见、情绪、环境、偏见，那么减法完成后剩下的就是一个清晰、真实、客观的世界。

这种心态如此普遍，以至于无法摆脱它。

“自古以来，[这种]理性就被用来使自己摆脱周围环境的单调和抑郁。 令人难以理解的是，它曾经被用来逃避一切，但现在这种逃避是如此成功，以至于现在浪漫主义者试图逃避“一切”。”4Marginnote zmm4Pirsig, R. 禅宗与摩托车维修艺术。 复古 2004 年；页数 65–66 ↩

教宗写道：“这些反应的明显客观性可能导致我们忽视这样一个事实，即它们反映了设计和训练这些反应的人的文化假设。”5Marginnote mh1005Magnifica humanitas, § 100 ↩ 假装无处可谈并不是没有偏见，而是其本身的偏见，是建设者所持有的偏见，隐藏得足够好，以至于他们向自己隐藏了它。 只有一种观点可以说是客观的，而且我们任何人都无法直接理解。

下面的路

“这些系统只是模仿人类智能的某些功能。 在此过程中，它们通常在速度和计算能力方面超越人类智能，在许多领域提供切实的好处。 然而这种能力仍然完全依赖于数据处理。 (…) 他们可能会模仿语言、行为和分析技能，甚至模拟同理心和理解力，但他们不明白自己产生了什么，因为他们缺乏人类增长智慧所需的情感、关系和精神视角。”6Marginnote mh996Magnifica humanitas, § 99 ↩

Pirsig 在《禅宗与摩托车维修艺术》第 6 章中用了很大一部分时间以几种不同的方式拆开摩托车。7Marginnote zmm27Z&AMM，第 17 页。 66–68 ↩ 他绘制的分区没有焊接到机器上。 将摩托车雕刻成零件并没有唯一正确的方法；一个人选择从哪里切入，他是根据他已经理解的东西、他以前见过的失败的东西、他碰巧关心的东西来选择的。 骑手可能关心根据功能的拆分，机械师可能关心根据其组成组件的拆分，零件供应商可能会刻意遵循工厂规定的零件编号方案来进行自己的拆分。 机器附带的手册隐藏了所有这些，以客观的旁观者的声音写成，就好像没有人在背后支持一样——当然有人支持。 没有发现摩托车躺在田野里。 人们让它们奔跑，并留下痕迹。

机器没有这样的路径——或者更确切地说，这就是整个麻烦，它假装自己没有这样的路径。 人工智能模仿了这种结构，但由于它以完全不同的方式“推理”，它无法自行产生它。 形式被复制而没有产生它的理解。 它是一个伟大的伪装者——在某种程度上，这就是它的本来面目——所以当你阅读人工智能生成的内容时，无论是散文还是代码，常常会感到某种不安。 内容可能在任何有意义的意义上都是正确的，看起来是正确的，但同时它似乎完全没有任何底层结构。 人类自然地会使用类比来思考、推理、体验和交谈；当超过一定的最低质量阈值时，很明显，文字背后存在某种结构，而这种结构是机器无法奠定的。

这条路并非完全不存在。 当您生成代码或散文时，必须将一些知识放入该生成中，而该输入（即大多数情况下的代理提示）是一个人工制品，它像任何其他人类创造性工作一样，在其下面有一条路径。 困难的是，当审查人工智能生成的代码或阅读人工智能生成的散文时，你得到的是输出而不是输入，两者脱节得越远——人类判断的最后一点和最终的人工制品之间的差距越大——就越难弄清楚那条路是什么，或者是否一开始就有一条路。

当你阅读时，你会本能地寻找下面的结构——为什么在这里而不是那里，看到了什么和搁置什么，作者对他的假设不确定的地方。 当你无法判断你所看到的作品是一位细心的作家，还是一只随机的鹦鹉时，你就无法判断其结构是否存在，或者其中投入了多少人类智慧。 这就是为什么阅读你已经记录的人工智能内容是如此令人疲惫不堪。 你在猜测，甚至在寻找你不知道的东西。

签名及其隐藏的内容

“这就是问责制变得至关重要的地方：确定谁必须对决策‘负责’、证明其合理性、监督决策，并在必要时挑战决策并补救造成的任何伤害。”11Marginnote mh10511Magnifica humanitas, § 105 ↩

当我为一家大型专业服务客户开发一个项目时，我们制定了惯例，以确保每一行代码都可以追溯到最终负责的人：代码行存在于标有 Jira 票证的提交中，票证带有主题专家的签名，他们确保了需求和业务逻辑的正确性，并且它们存在于由经理签名的更大的史诗中。 当某件事发生得足够严重时，该链条中的每个人都会接到电话并致力于修复。 我的一些同事认为这不健康，并说我们应该进行无可指责的事后分析。

这些天我们有它们：“哦，克劳德是这样写的。 你也有这个问题，只需提示它进行修复即可。”

我注意到，现在人们花费了大量的精力来摆脱机器的输出。 与我一起工作的一些人不想承认某个特定的提交是由人工智能编写的，因为承认这一点就会引发一个问题：他们是否完全理解这个问题。 因此，他们用自己的名字在提交上签名，省略了共同作者，并让读者来决定他正在看的是一个有能力的程序员的作品还是一个语言模型。 暗示同事的工作是人工智能生成的也是不礼貌的，因为这个暗示意味着他没有思考。 所以这个问题从来没有被问过。 整个事情都消失了，我们忘记了在工作交给机器之前理解最后存在的水平，或者它是否曾经存在过。

这正是通谕要求我们保持“确定谁必须对决策负责的可能性”的可能性。 讨论战争的通谕坚持认为“不允许将致命或其他不可逆转的决定委托给人工系统。”12Marginnote mh19812Magnifica humanitas, § 198 ↩ 这一原则并不局限于战场。 所有系统都应该有一条责任链，最终以一个人为终点，即使只是出于尊重和礼貌的原因，而不知从何而来的声音的麻烦在于，它让这条责任链在寻找其他人时以虚无结束，就好像它以你为终点一样。

不知从何而来的声音之所以具有诱惑力，正因为它是危险的：它不知从何而来，所以没有人可以信任，没有人可以责备，也没有人可以问“你是怎么知道的？” 教宗说，技术展现了技术创造者的性格。 困扰我们的不是它所呈现的性格，而是我们多么容易学会用一种根本不承认任何创造者的声音来建造。
